stem.text: The molecular formula of benzene is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>. The six carbon atoms in benzene form a six-membered ring.
State the C–C–H bond angle in benzene and the hybridisation of each carbon atom.

explanation.text: Each carbon in benzene forms three σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H) and has no lone pair, so the three bonds are trigonal planar at 120°. Three σ bonds from one carbon use three sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals; the remaining unhybridised p orbital forms part of the delocalised π system.
Both the angle and the hybridisation are needed for the single mark.

reasoningChain: Count σ bonds around each C: 3, no lone pairs.
Trigonal planar: 120°.
Three hybrid orbitals: sp<sup>2</sup>.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving 109.5° and sp<sup>3</sup>, treating benzene like cyclohexane.
Giving the angle correctly but writing sp or sp<sup>3</sup>, or leaving one of the two lines blank.

stem.text: The bonds between neighbouring carbon atoms in benzene involve two types of orbital overlap, giving σ and π bonds.
Name the orbitals involved, and describe the orbital overlap, in σ and π bonds.

guidance: CON s orbital unless clearly referring to C-H, where you ignore s orbital.
A orbital type written in overlap space if not written in ‘orbitals involved’ space. Otherwise consider only orbitals on the ‘orbitals involved lines’ and only overlap on the ‘orbital overlap’ lines.
Read ‘6p orbitals’ as the number of p orbitals.

points.text: head on / direct / end-on / linear / acceptable description

explanation.text: A C–C σ bond in benzene forms from two sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals, one from each carbon, overlapping head-on along the line between the nuclei. The π bonding comes from the unhybridised p orbitals, one on each carbon, perpendicular to the ring; they overlap sideways above and below the plane, forming the delocalised π system.
The MS marks two points for one mark and all four for two. An s orbital is only right for the C–H bond, so mentioning s for the C–C σ bond contradicts the answer.

reasoningChain: σ: sp<sup>2</sup> + sp<sup>2</sup>, overlap head-on (end-on).
π: p + p, overlap sideways.
Write each item on its own answer line.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing s and p (or s and sp<sup>2</sup>) for the C–C σ bond; s orbitals are only involved in C–H bonds.
Swapping the overlap descriptions, saying σ bonds form by sideways overlap.
Saying the π bond uses sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals instead of unhybridised p orbitals.

stem.text: Figure 7.1 describes a four-step synthesis of phenol, starting with benzene.

stem.caption: Figure 7.1
stem.alt: Benzene, reaction 1, G (nitrobenzene, C6H5NO2), reaction 2, an empty box labelled J; reaction 3 (downward arrow) gives K, benzenediazonium chloride (C6H5N+≡N Cl–); reaction 4 (arrow pointing left) gives phenol, C6H5OH.

stem.text: State the reagents and conditions for reaction 1 in Figure 7.1.

guidance: Conc, con or c seen once.

explanation.text: Reaction 1 is the nitration of benzene. The syllabus conditions are a mixture of concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> and concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at 25–60 °C. The sulfuric acid generates the NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile; above about 60 °C further nitration becomes significant.

reasoningChain: G is nitrobenzene, so reaction 1 is nitration.
Reagents: conc HNO<sub>3</sub> and conc H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
Condition: a temperature between 25 and 60 °C.

inferredMistakes.text: Omitting H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or the word concentrated.
Writing ‘heat’ or ‘reflux’ without a temperature in the 25–60 °C range; the MS ignores these words.
Writing dilute or aqueous nitric acid, which contradicts the answer.

stem.text: The reagents and conditions for reaction 2 are concentrated HCl and Sn, heated under reflux.
Draw the structure of compound J in Figure 7.1.

explanation.text: Sn and concentrated HCl reduce the –NO<sub>2</sub> group of nitrobenzene to –NH<sub>2</sub>, giving phenylamine. In the acidic mixture the amine is actually present as the phenylammonium ion, which is why C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> or its chloride is also accepted. J then reacts with HNO<sub>2</sub> to form the diazonium salt K.

reasoningChain: Reaction 2 is a reduction of NO<sub>2</sub>.
–NO<sub>2</sub> becomes –NH<sub>2</sub>: J is phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.
Check: phenylamine is the starting material for a diazonium salt, which matches K.

inferredMistakes.text: Drawing the ring with –NH– or –NO, a partial reduction product.
Drawing an extra substituent on the ring, e.g. chlorobenzene from the HCl.

stem.text: State the reagents and conditions for reactions 3 and 4 in Figure 7.1.

guidance: A [1] for all correct reagents or both correct temperatures.
M2 CON addition of NaOH but ignore acids.

explanation.text: Reaction 3 is diazotisation: phenylamine with nitrous acid, made in situ from NaNO<sub>2</sub> and dilute HCl, below 10 °C. The low temperature is needed because the diazonium salt decomposes when warm.
Reaction 4 uses exactly that instability: warming the aqueous diazonium salt above 10 °C makes it lose N<sub>2</sub> and react with water to give phenol.

reasoningChain: Reaction 3: J (phenylamine) to K (diazonium salt) needs HNO<sub>2</sub> (NaNO<sub>2</sub> + HCl) at 0–10 °C.
Reaction 4: K to phenol needs water and warming above 10 °C.

inferredMistakes.text: Writing HNO<sub>3</sub> or NaNO<sub>3</sub> (nitric acid / nitrate) instead of HNO<sub>2</sub> / NaNO<sub>2</sub>.
Giving the temperatures the wrong way round, or omitting the temperature for one reaction.
Adding NaOH in reaction 4, which is the condition for coupling with phenol, not for making phenol; the MS treats it as a contradiction.

stem.text: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride, CH3COCl, in the presence of an AlCl3 catalyst.
In this reaction, the electrophile is the CH<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>O ion.
Complete the mechanism in Figure 7.2 for this reaction.
Include all relevant curly arrows and charges.

stem.caption: Figure 7.2
stem.alt: Benzene and the electrophile CH3C+=O on the left, an arrow to an empty box labelled ‘organic intermediate’, an arrow to the product C6H5COCH3, followed by ‘+ ......’.

guidance: CON curly arrow from H rather than middle of bond for M3
‘Horseshoe’ must include C3, C4 and C5, may include C2 and / or C6, CON including C1.
+ charge must be above a line joining C2 and C6.
I connectivity of side group if drawn as OCCH3 for M2.
A HCl for M3 if Cl– introduced earlier.

points.text: M1 curly arrow from within / touching hexagon towards C+
M3 curly arrow from C–H bond goes within hexagon and H+

markScheme.note: The MS answer column prints the intermediate drawing beside M2; the Guidance column prints the same intermediate with carbons numbered 1–6. Both drawings are joined in the figure (answer left, Guidance right).

figure.alt: From the MS: left, the intermediate with H and C(=O)CH3 on one ring carbon and a horseshoe-shaped partial ring with + inside covering the other five carbons; right, from the Guidance column, the same intermediate with ring carbons numbered 1 (the carbon bearing H and COCH3) to 6.

explanation.text: This is Friedel–Crafts acylation, an electrophilic substitution. Step 1: a pair of electrons from the delocalised ring attacks the C<sup>+</sup> of CH<sub>3</sub>C<sup>+</sup>O, forming a C–C bond. The intermediate has the new carbon (C1) bonded to both H and COCH<sub>3</sub>, and the remaining four π electrons spread over the other five ring carbons, shown as a horseshoe with + inside.

Step 2: the C–H bond on C1 breaks and its electrons go back into the ring, restoring the delocalised system and releasing H<sup>+</sup>, the other product on the answer line. Restoring aromatic stability is why substitution happens rather than addition.
The horseshoe must not pass through C1, which is now sp<sup>3</sup>, and the + goes in the open part of the horseshoe, on the side away from C1.

reasoningChain: Arrow 1: from the ring (inside the hexagon) to the C<sup>+</sup>.
Draw the intermediate: H and COCH<sub>3</sub> on the same carbon, horseshoe over C2–C6 with + inside, not through C1.
Arrow 2: from the middle of the C–H bond into the ring.
Write H<sup>+</sup> as the second product.

inferredMistakes.text: Starting the second curly arrow from the H atom rather than the C–H bond, which contradicts M3.
Drawing the horseshoe through the sp<sup>3</sup> carbon (C1) or leaving out the + charge.
Drawing the first curly arrow from the C<sup>+</sup> to the ring (wrong direction), or adding an arrow from C=O.
Writing HCl as the product without having shown AlCl<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> or Cl<sup>–</sup> anywhere.

stem.text: The product of the reaction shown in Figure 7.2, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, can be oxidised by heating with alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>.
The reaction mixture is then acidified. Benzoic acid, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH, is produced.
Complete the equation for the overall reaction, where [O] represents one atom of oxygen from the oxidising agent.

explanation.text: Hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> oxidises the whole side chain of an alkylbenzene down to –COOH on the ring. Here the side chain –COCH<sub>3</sub> has two carbons; the one attached to the ring becomes COOH and the CH<sub>3</sub> carbon leaves as CO<sub>2</sub>.
Balance: left C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O + n[O]; right C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O = C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>5</sub>. So n = 4.

reasoningChain: The lost carbon leaves as CO<sub>2</sub>; the leftover H leaves as H<sub>2</sub>O.
Count oxygen on the right: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5; the left already has 1.
So 4[O].

inferredMistakes.text: Writing CH<sub>4</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>OH as a product, so the equation is not an oxidation.
Giving 3[O] by forgetting the oxygen in water, or 5[O] by forgetting the oxygen already in C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>.

stem.text: Figure 7.3 describes a two-step synthesis of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH.
C6H5COCH3 is treated with two reagents, firstly reagent M and secondly reagent N, producing C6H5COOH.

stem.caption: Figure 7.3
stem.alt: C6H5COCH3 drawn as a benzene ring with C(=O)CH3, then two arrows labelled M and N, then C6H5COOH drawn as a benzene ring with C(=O)OH.

stem.text: Identify M and N, neither contains MnO4– or Cr2O72–.

after: (pass alternative (correct) method to TL for advice, e.g. LiAlH4 then alkaline I2 followed by acid)

explanation.text: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> contains a CH<sub>3</sub>CO– group, so it gives the tri-iodomethane (iodoform) reaction with alkaline iodine. The CH<sub>3</sub> becomes CHI<sub>3</sub> (yellow precipitate) and the rest of the molecule is left as the carboxylate, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COO<sup>–</sup>.
The carboxylate is the salt of a weak acid, so adding any strong acid (N) protonates it to benzoic acid. M2 is unconditional, so the acid scores even if M is wrong.
The MS also notes that other correct routes, e.g. LiAlH<sub>4</sub> then alkaline I<sub>2</sub> followed by acid, should be referred to the Team Leader.

reasoningChain: Spot the CH<sub>3</sub>CO– group, which allows the iodoform reaction.
M: I<sub>2</sub> with NaOH(aq) gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COO<sup>–</sup> + CHI<sub>3</sub>.
N: dilute acid, e.g. HCl, gives C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving acidified or alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> or K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>, which the question excludes.
Giving iodine without the alkali (or alkali without iodine) for M.
Adding extra reagents, which the MS treats as a contradiction.
